paras: The whipping and expulsion of Black residents of Cooper, Texas, was a pair of night floggings in June 1903 in which six Black men in Cooper, Delta County, were whipped a week apart and the men flogged were compelled to leave the county. A Dallas dispatch said the men were charged with criticizing the life sentence given a Black man for attempted assault, while a New Orleans dispatch described those whipped as loafers and petty criminals driven out by "the Regulars." Northern and Southern papers carried the story as part of a reported Southern drive to push "disorderly" Black people north.

About two weeks before the main flogging, a Black man named Walker had been tried and given a life sentence for attempting to assault a white woman, according to the Dallas report. For a week before the reports, notices posted "in conspicuous places" warned Black residents to leave Cooper "or take the consequences."

Three Black men were whipped first; a week later, on a Wednesday night, three men the Dallas dispatch called "negro leaders" were taken from their homes and "severely flogged." The papers give no calendar date, but the dispatch was dated Thursday, June 25, which places the second raid most likely on June 24 and the first about June 17. The flogged men were compelled to leave the county, and they were said to be charged with "insolent criticism" of Walker's trial and sentence.

The New York correspondent of La Correspondencia de Puerto Rico wrote that the men left in haste and that their only alleged offence was objecting that another Black man had not had the full protection of the law.

On Thursday night a meeting of "leading white and black citizens" was held at Cooper, where the white men said that "the well-behaved" could remain and be protected but that the "worthless, insolent and dangerous negroes would have to go." Officers were reported to be searching for the men who did the flogging. In the New Orleans account the meeting took place at the court house, and Black residents who had complained to the authorities about notices on their houses promised to help keep down "the lawless element" and report lawbreakers. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial of the floggers was found.

The New York Sun first carried the Dallas dispatch on June 26 as a brief item, "Negroes Ordered to Lea[v]e Cooper County, Texas," at the end of a long report on rioting in Wilmington, Delaware. The next day the Sun printed the New Orleans dispatch as "Bad Negroes Coming North," which presented Cooper as the start in Texas of a movement to rid Southern towns of "the disorderly negro element" and unload criminals on the North. The Minneapolis Journal commented the same day that such expulsions were "right in line with the police policy" of moving criminals on, and found it "reassuring" that orderly Black residents at Cooper had been pledged protection.

The Dallas version ran in Oregon in the Corvallis Times on July 1 and in Missouri on July 2, where the Mexico Missouri Message headlined it "Insolent Negroes Given a Flogging" and "Citizens Warn Worthless Blacks to Leave Cooper, Texas." On July 8 two South Carolina papers, the Keowee Courier and the Anderson Intelligencer, reprinted the Sun's New Orleans item. Of the papers found, only La Correspondencia de Puerto Rico treated the whippings as persecution, saying the men were beaten "inhumanamente" and setting the case beside more than ten recent lynchings and plans for Black emigration to Liberia. No Black newspaper account of the episode was found.

The Dallas report called the men whipped "negro leaders" punished for criticizing a sentence and said the notices went up a week before the second raid. The New Orleans dispatch called them "negro loafers, negro sneak thieves and petty criminals," said notices appeared afterward on the houses of "better class negroes," and reported that an investigation traced those notices to "mischievous boys." The Dallas account is the more specific of the two, naming Walker, the meeting and the search for the floggers, while the New Orleans version came inside a regional argument for expelling Black criminals.

reader.title: Whipping and expulsion of Black residents of Cooper, Texas
bases: Unnamed men, called 'the Regulars' in one dispatch, took Black men from their homes at night, whipped them and forced them out of the county after notices warning Black residents to leave (A1, A5, A2).

Two independent dispatches, from Dallas (A1, A5) and New Orleans (A2), agree that Black men at Cooper, Delta County, were whipped and made to leave, though they disagree on who the men were, why they were whipped and who posted the notices.

accounts.label: Dallas wire report
accounts.gist: Notices warned Black residents to leave Cooper for a week; three 'negro leaders' were flogged on Wednesday night after three others had been whipped a week before, and all were forced out for criticizing Walker's sentence. A citizens' meeting followed and officers were hunting the floggers.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: 'The Regulars' whipped and ordered out Cooper's Black 'loafers' and petty criminals; notices later placed on the houses of 'better class negroes' were found to be the work of boys, and a court-house meeting pledged protection to orderly Black residents.

accounts.label: New York correspondent of La Correspondencia de Puerto Rico
accounts.gist: Retells the Dallas facts, saying the men were beaten 'inhumanamente' and that their only alleged offence was objecting that another Black man had not had the full protection of the law.

framing.detail: The Sun ran the Dallas item under 'Negroes Ordered to Lea[v]e Cooper County, Texas' as a tail to its Wilmington riot report, without comment.
The Sun's 'Bad Negroes Coming North. Southern Cities Driving Out the Loafers and Criminals' cast the whippings as part of a Southern movement against the 'disorderly negro element'.
The Minneapolis Journal called expulsions 'right in line with the police policy' of moving criminals on, while finding the Cooper pledge to orderly Black residents 'reassuring'.
The Mexico Missouri Message headlined the Dallas wire 'Insolent Negroes Given a Flogging' and 'Citizens Warn Worthless Blacks to Leave Cooper, Texas'.
Two South Carolina weeklies reprinted the Sun's New Orleans item on July 8.
La Correspondencia de Puerto Rico said the men were beaten 'inhumanamente' and whipped 'de una manera despiadada', placing the case among recent lynchings and Black emigration plans.
